First, check flame test (cost 1 mL). Use perform_flame_test.

We have unknown salt dissolved in water, 20 mL sample. Flame test gave yellow flame. Yellow flame typical of sodium (Na+). Could also be potassium gives lilac, calcium orange-red, etc. Yellow is characteristic of Na+. So cation likely Na+. Could also be some other that gives yellow? Lithium gives crimson, etc. So Na+.

Now need anion. Use reagents to test. We have limited sample volume 20 mL. Use small volumes.

We can test with AgNO3 to precipitate halides: AgCl (white), AgBr (pale yellow), AgI (yellow). Also test with BaCl2? Actually Ba(NO3)2 to precipitate sulfate (BaSO4 white), carbonate (BaCO3 white), chromate (BaCrO4 yellow). Use HCl acid to test for carbonate (CO2 effervescence). Use H2S acidic to test for metal sulfides (but cation is Na, not relevant). Use NH4Cl etc.

We suspect anion could be Cl-, Br-, I-, SO4^2-, NO3-, CO3^2-, HCO3-, PO4^3-, etc.

We have reagents: AgNO3, Ba(NO3)2, Pb(NO3)2, HNO3, HCl, KOH, H2SO4, NH3, NH4Cl, BUFFER_9, NH4I, H2S(acidic), (NH4)2S, (NH4)2CO3, (NH4)2HPO4, K2CrO4, FeCl3.

We can start with AgNO3 test: add few drops to sample, observe precipitate color.

We have unknown inorganic salt, pure cation and anion. Sample 20 mL. Flame test gave yellow flame => likely Na+ (sodium) gives bright yellow. Could also K gives lilac, Ca orange-red, Ba green, etc. Yellow is characteristic of Na+. So cation likely Na+. Next test with AgNO3 gave white precipitate. That suggests anion forms insoluble Ag salt: possible Cl-, Br-, I- (AgCl white, AgBr pale yellow, AgI yellow). White precipitate suggests AgCl. Could also Ag2SO4? That's white but less common. So likely Cl-.

We should confirm with other reagents: test with Ba(NO3)2 for sulfate (white precipitate). If no precipitate, not sulfate. Also test with Pb(NO3)2 for halides (PbCl2 white, PbI2 yellow). Could test with HCl acid to see solubility of precipitate.

We have used 1 mL sample in flame test (non-consumptive) and 1 mL in AgNO3 test (consumed). Sample remaining 18 mL.
